newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Timorese protest for second day, stone legislature.
newsitem.headline: Timorese protest for second day, stone legislature.

text.p: Students in East Timor demonstrated for a second day on Wednesday over Indonesian criticism of Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, with some youths stoning the local legislature.
Witnesses said some demonstrators pelted the legislature building with stones before moving on to the seafront governor's office. They later dispersed without further incident.
"There were some windows broken (at the legislature), but not many," East Timor's deputy police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto told Reuters by telephone from the capital Dili.
"There were no other incidents. The situation is under control. It is calm and normal again," he said, adding that there had been no arrests.
"There was a lot of tension, but I believe the restraint of the security forces helped students to keep their cool," a diplomatic source in close contact with Dili said.

In Jakarta, four East Timorese who sought political asylum in the Spanish embassy on Tuesday were expected to leave for Portugal on Wednesday evening, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said.
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
More than 1,000 students and high school pupils had gathered in the morning at the University of East Timor in central Dili.
Several hundred police in riot gear were deployed in the streets but police and residents said there was no confrontation.
Sources in the city said the demonstrations were apparently sparked by strong Indonesian criticism of Bishop Belo, who is highly respected in mainly-Catholic East Timor.

Television footage on Tuesday night showed a protest in Jakarta by more than 2,000 members of youth groups allied to the ruling Golkar party demanding the bishop be expelled for remarks he was reported to have made in a German magazine interview.
He has been reported as saying in the interview with Der Spiegel that Indonesian troops had trampled on East Timor's independence "and treated us like dogs".
Belo, who flew to Jakarta on Monday for an annual meeting of Catholic bishops, has refused to comment until he sees the full transcript of the interview.
East Timorese students had staged a protest at the Dili university on Tuesday, the fifth anniversary of the shooting of at least 50 demonstrators in the city by Indonesian troops.
College authorities had closed the university on Tuesday after a heated debate between students and the official National Human Rights Commission the previous day.
It reopened on Wednesday.
"Today we expected to have the mid-semester examinations, but evidently it is a bit difficult," vice-rector Armindo Maia told Reuters.
Sources in Dili said a group of students had presented a petition to the East Timor legislature.

In their meeting with the Human Rights Commission, students had handed over a statement saying that attacks on Belo were deliberately designed to discredit him and promote instability in the territory.
Belo was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel peace prize last month with self-exiled East-Timorese born activist Jose Ramos Horta.
